newsitem.title: USA: U.S. science agency adds rural funds to Internet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. science agency adds rural funds to Internet.

text.p: Seeking to head off a political tussle over appropriations for the government's "Next Generation Internet," the National Science Foundation said this week it would pay to connect universities in 18 rural states to the project.

In a July 17 letter to Sen. Conrad Burns, Republican of Montana, NSF director Neal Lane said his agency would augment grants to rural states under its existing Experimental Programme to Stimulate Competitive Research, known as EPSCoR.

"Rural institutions should not be unfairly penalised by disproportionately high connection costs to high performance networks," Lane wrote. "To ameliorate this problem, the National Science Foundation will augment some grants for high performance connections to help defray the high costs of links for rural institutions."

The Next Generation Internet project, announced with great fanfare by President Clinton during last year's campaign, aims to send data at up to 1,000 times the speed of today's Internet. Higher speed and improved reliability could spur a host of new uses for the network, some with live sound and video feeds.

Lane's letter follows criticism of the agency last month by senators who complained that the agency planned to send most of the new Internet project's money to schools in a few big states like California and Massachusetts.

The agency already gives qualified schools $350,000 to connect to the fastest portion of the Internet, called the "very high speed Backbone Network Service," which will form the core of the Next Generation Internet. Lane said schools in the rural states will be eligible for an additional $200,000 each.
Burns, who organised a hearing June 3 to air the concerns of rural states about the project, praised the additional funding.
"These grants should provide a great opportunity to level the playing field and include rural states in all aspects of future Internet development," Burns said.
A House Appropriations Committee report on funding for the NSF released this month included $23 million for the Internet project, a $13 million increase from the amount requested.

"The Committee action is in recognition of recent changes in this multi-agency effort," the report said. The Clinton administration plans to spend $100 million a year, divided among several agencies, on the project.

The 18 states included in EPSCoR are Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Vermont, West Virginia and Wyoming.
